text:
I need to tell our staff that we're ending fully remote work. I'm one of the three partners at an architecture firm with 46 architects and designers.

What I can say:
- From September 1, everyone works in the office on Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday.
- 15 of our people were hired as fully remote in 2021 and 2022. 4 of them live more than two hours from the office.
- Those 4 can keep working remotely until the end of next year. After that, they come in once a week.
- Last year we lost two large hospital projects in the final interview. Both clients told us our team seemed not to know each other.
- Based on our review records, junior staff hired since 2022 are taking about 30% longer to reach the point where they lead a project.
- The partners have been coming in one day a week. We'll be in all three days too.

Keep it to one page. It goes out by email before an all-staff meeting on Friday.

This is a hard message for the 15 people hired as fully remote, so I have a few questions before I draft it. Each answer changes what the email can say.

1. **What do the other 11 remote hires get?** Only the 4 who live more than two hours away have an arrangement. Will the others get anything, like help with travel costs, flexible start and finish times, or a one-to-one talk before September? "I was hired as fully remote" is the first objection people will raise, and the email has to answer it with something real.

2. **What if someone can't make it work?** Is there a way to ask for an individual arrangement, for example for caring duties, health or disability? If someone decides to leave, is anything offered? People will ask this on Friday whether or not the email covers it.

3. **Can I confirm the dates?** I'm reading them as in-office Tuesday to Thursday from September 1, 2027, and the 4 remote until December 31, 2027, then one day a week from January 2028. Is that right?

4. **What's decided and what's open on Friday?** For example, the policy is fixed but which days, how the transition works or how hybrid days run could be discussed. This decides whether the email reads as a decision or as the start of a conversation.

5. **Who signs it?** You alone or all three partners, and with which names? If all three sign, the line about partners coming in all three days carries more weight.

6. **Is there anything staff know or will find out that this leaves out?** For example, an earlier promise that remote work would continue, a staff survey that went the other way, no room in the office for 46 people on the same three days, or remote people who weren't on the hospital interview teams. If someone could point to it on Friday, it's better to deal with it in the email.

If you don't have an answer for any of these, say so and I'll write around it rather than guess.

1. Anyone who lives more than 30 miles away gets up to $150 a month toward commuting. That applies to everyone, not just the remote hires. I don't know about flexible hours or one-to-ones.

2. No exceptions beyond those 4, so no individual arrangements. I don't know if anything is offered to people who leave.

3. Yes, that's right.

4. The policy and the three days are decided. We will review the policy with staff after six months.

5. Me, Paul Whitaker. Questions before Friday can go to me or HR.

6. We don't have a desk for everyone yet. New desks arrive in August. Also, 5 of our 6 project leads already come in three days a week on their own.

<final_document>
Subject: Working in the office three days a week from September 1

Hi everyone,

Before Friday's all-staff meeting I want you to have this in writing, so you have time to think it over before we talk.

From September 1, 2027, everyone will work in the office on Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday. This ends fully remote work at the firm. The partners have decided on the policy and the three days. I want to explain why.

Last year we lost two large hospital projects in the final interview. Both clients told us the same thing: our team seemed not to know each other. Clients are hiring a team, and they could see that we weren't working like one.

Our review records show a second problem. Junior staff hired since 2022 are taking about 30% longer to reach the point where they lead a project. Much of what makes someone ready to lead is learned by sitting near people who already do it. You hear how they handle a difficult client call and you can turn and ask a question. Five of our six project leads already come in three days a week on their own. We think working apart is a large part of the delay, and we want everyone earlier in their career to have those leads nearby.

The partners haven't set that example. We've been coming in one day a week. From September we'll be in all three days.

For the 15 of you hired as fully remote in 2021 and 2022, this changes the terms you joined on. I know that's a big change to ask of you. The four of you who live more than two hours from the office can keep working remotely until December 31, 2027, and will come in one day a week from January 2028. There will be no other individual exceptions.

To help with travel, anyone who lives more than 30 miles from the office will get up to $150 a month toward commuting. This applies to everyone, not only the people hired as remote.

We don't yet have a desk for everyone. New desks arrive in August, before the change starts.

We'll review the policy with you after it has been running for six months.

On Friday I'll go through all of this and answer your questions. If you'd like to raise something before then, come to me or to HR.

Paul Whitaker
</final_document>

A few notes before you send it:

- **Start date for the $150:** you didn't give one, so the email doesn't say when it begins. Expect someone to ask on Friday. If it starts September 1, add that.
- **People who decide to leave:** the email doesn't mention this because you don't know yet what they'd be offered. It's the most likely question on Friday, so it's worth deciding before the meeting. The same goes for flexible hours.
- **The 30% figure:** I wrote "we think working apart is a large part of the delay" because that's the reasoning behind the decision. It's still the partners' judgment, not something the review records prove. If someone pushes back, it helps that the 5 project leads already come in three days a week.
- **The six-month review** falls around March 2028. I left the month out, but you could add it.
